newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fear of Hong Kong's handover exaggerated - poll.
newsitem.headline: Fear of Hong Kong's handover exaggerated - poll.

text.p: Fears about Hong Kong's future after the British colony returns to Chinese rule next year tend to be exaggerated by head offices of Western multinationals, according to a survey of corporate managers in Asia.
The survey of common head office misconceptions about Asia was conducted by the Hong Kong-based Political & Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).

It found that many Western head office managers tended to be excessively cautious about doing business in Hong Kong ahead of the July 1997 handover, while local businessmen viewed it in terms of offering new opportunities.

PERC said Hong Kong's business environment was more likely to be hurt by high costs than heavy-handed treatment by China, and companies that showed excessive caution now could end up losing their competitive advantage.

The survey, published in the latest edition of PERC's Asian Intelligence report, found the gap between head office expectations and the realities on the ground widest in Indonesia and closest to the mark in Singapore.

Managers in Indonesia said they had to cope with head office ignorance of the nature and extent of bureaucratic red tape and of the hardships of working in a country where traffic jams, pollution and general uncertainty were daily realities.
Head offices viewed Singapore as having an anti-Western and authoritarian government and did not recognise the difficulties in recruiting and retaining staff here.
"Such head offices are thus surprised to find that politics and business in Singapore are generally kept quite separate," PERC said.

The chief complaint among Malaysian managers was their head office's tendency to underestimate the sophistication of the local business community and the country's recent economic and social progress.
PERC said head office managers were overly concerned about the frequent changes in Thailand's government and the current slowdown in economic growth.
"Notably, they ignore the discipline that has always characterised the Thai financial system, the effective management of the currency, and the high level of domestic savings," it said.
